items.summary: Signal announced protections that block screenshots on iOS 27 and prevent the built-in Siri and Gemini assistants from capturing Signal conversations on supported Android devices. The measures follow a May 2025 feature blocking Microsoft's Recall screenshot-capturing tool on Windows 11, with president Meredith Whittaker describing OS-level features such as Siri's Onscreen Awareness and Google's Gemini Intelligence as able to capture chat content as it appears on screen. Signal stated its engineers spent months reverse-engineering how AI systems access app data in order to block all verified extraction pathways, though the company warned that agents embedded deep in operating systems could still reach conversations through other methods—something Whittaker called an existential threat—and noted macOS currently offers no screenshot-blocking protection, recommending users add the app to the Excluded Apps list under System Settings > Siri. Signal did not provide specific version numbers and said protections activate automatically when possible; it recommended iOS users upgrade and verify Block Siri AI in Settings > App Security, while Android enables Screen Security upon detecting an assistant attempt. The article also included unrelated promotional content for Microsoft 365/Google Workspace email security scans with a 14-day read-only option.
items.title: Signal Blocks Screenshots and AI Captures on iOS 27 and Android

items.summary: In a November 2026 interview, Yale assistant professor of American studies Julián Posada discussed his book Platform Extractivism: Data Work and the People Powering Artificial Intelligence (University of California Press), which centers on Venezuelans who became major data workers during the country's economic collapse and the COVID-19 pandemic. Posada argues that AI's promised freedom from work has not materialized for most people, as gig-style terms now extend to high-paid professions like medicine and law—for example, Scale AI (Meta-backed) recruited cardiologists at roughly $180–$200 an hour under the same terms of service copied from its Venezuelan-era platform Remotasks. He attributes Venezuela's prominence in data work to a combination of hyperinflation pushing workers toward dollar-denominated platforms, pre-crisis government infrastructure like computers and subsidized internet, and what he calls 'epistemic dominance,' where instructions imposed on workers encode Northern frameworks—such as US census racial categories or First Amendment-based hate-speech definitions—that often did not fit Latin American realities. Posada notes the population is invisible: some interviewees maintained 10–15 rotating accounts per family, and minors used grandparents' identities to authenticate work, so even platforms could not accurately count their workers. He documents worker organizing through closed Telegram and WhatsApp groups that provided trusted brokers for exchanging digital currencies like AirTM (paid in cash due to sanctions), shared exploits to increase earnings, and insurance against scams, though he cautions many of these groups likely disbanded as Venezuela's situation improved—illustrated by his bookend interviewee Roberto, who left data work when facial-recognition authentication failed him because the models were inaccurate for darker-skinned people. Posada frames gig-style labor spreading to skilled sectors as evidence that rising productivity has not reduced hours or narrowed wage gaps, and he hopes regulation will come from destination countries like the United States while emphasizing worker organizing alongside top-down policy.
items.title: Yale Scholar Julián Posada on the Invisible Data Workers Behind AI

items.summary:
At a conference in Bangkok titled the Second Regional Networking Visit for Platform Workers in Asia, organized by the Just Economy and Labor Institute (JELI) and Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung (FES) Thailand, Tech Policy Press fellow Lam Le—based in Hanoi—took part as an attendee. During the event she met with workers and organizers and observed their discussions about organizing for recognition and labor rights among platform workers.

Le later discussed her observations on a podcast episode hosted by Justin Hendrix, which included recordings from delivery riders, remote outsourcing workers, artists, trade unionists, and researchers across India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand. These participants described their efforts to organize for recognition and labor rights within platform work.

The accompanying transcript of the episode was not yet available at the time of publication.
items.title: Asian Platform Workers Organize Across Borders for Labor Rights

items.summary: An 18-year-old Junior College Year 2 student, Adwin Lau Yu Tan, submitted a forum piece arguing that Singaporean graduates are taking longer on average to secure employment after graduation and urging society to normalize this shift. The author contends that familial discussions and social support still project the expectation of finding ideal jobs quickly upon graduation—an image reinforced by schoolteachers—that is unsustainable in reality. Because younger cohorts may face even longer searches, Lau recommends preparing for the transition productively through volunteering, courses, and short-term work, while calling on society to acknowledge job-search difficulties and ease the move toward independent income. The piece presents these views as advocacy rather than reported data; it offers no statistics or figures on actual search durations, so its claims remain grounded only in the author's perspective.
items.title: Student Advocates for Normalizing Extended Post-Graduation Job Searches in Singapore

items.summary: In response to Esther Yeo's letter questioning an over-emphasis on perfection in school-based examination marking, Ong Kong Hong of the Ministry of Education (MOE) explained that both science curriculum design and national examinations are intended to assess students' conceptual understanding and their ability to apply concepts across contexts. He stated that markers award points for demonstrated understanding rather than penalising missing keywords or imperfect diagrams when overall responses clearly reflect concept mastery; he cited a shared circuit question, noting that a parallel arrangement of bulbs would indicate comprehension of how an electrical system functions in context. On school-based assessments specifically, the MOE noted these are managed at the school level to align with their formative purpose and lower stakes, including mark scheme design and standardisation for consistency. He added that the ministry does not supply schools with mark schemes for such assessments, but acknowledged the specific school had already addressed Yeo's feedback directly. The response concluded by affirming MOE's ongoing provision of professional development to strengthen teachers' assessment literacy while framing continued support as aimed at fostering a love of learning in students.
items.title: MOE Clarifies Marking Practices Aim to Reward Conceptual Understanding Over Perfection

items.summary:
The text presents an argument that modern large language models are essentially compressors trained on vast data, and that tracking progress in training better compressors is the key to understanding advances in AI. OpenAI proposes establishing perplexity—equivalently cross-entropy loss—as a shared metric for comparing model developers and informing safety standards, arguing this transparency outweighs concerns about revealing competitive position. The text reports internal log-perplexity measurements on an internal codebase held-out dataset (a fixed snapshot), showing how the single metric has correlated with major capability leaps: GPT-2 (~0.99) forming coherent paragraphs, GPT-3 learning in context, GPT-3.5 (~0.99) enabling fluent conversation and original ChatGPT, GPT-4 (~0.91) enabling productive chain-of-thought reasoning, and losses below 0.8 coinciding with transformative capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics. The author notes these emergent capabilities were not predictable a priori at the specific thresholds met.

The text also addresses accelerating progress driven partly by AI contributing to its own development—specifically algorithmic research on pretraining rather than full recursive self-improvement—and cites OpenAI's experience posing open mathematical problems, where upgrading to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76 produced rapid groundbreaking results. The author extrapolates that an avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements could conceivably occur by 2027 and expects transformative capabilities in the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window.

OpenAI proposes industry norms for evaluating frontier models, red-teaming safety cases before first use, shared transparency standards, and common limits based on perplexity that developers commit to not crossing until monitoring capability reaches a concrete milestone such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitors. The text identifies four challenges with using perplexity: difficulty comparing across labs due to different evaluation datasets and data mixtures; detachment from actionable evaluations since it does not correspond directly to tasks of interest; failure to account for advances outside pretraining, notably that chain-of-thought reasoning increases capabilities without reducing perplexity; and an unknown floor below which progress may slow while smaller gains yield larger intelligence leaps. A footnote notes a steep acceleration in OpenAI's model losses during 2026, attributed mostly to long-term research and compute investments with only a smaller part from automation.
items.title: OpenAI Proposes Perplexity as a Shared Metric for Tracking and Pacing AI Progress

items.summary:
In a self-conducted test published under the byline of Polly Hudson, an author manually disabled AI features on her iPhone—switching off Apple Intelligence in settings, marking Siri as unassisted, and deselecting suggested replies to texts and emails—but reported that proposed responses continued to appear. Bored during bus travel, she deliberately answered messages from her husband using these suggestions to determine whether he would notice the artificial origin; according to the account, he did not detect a difference even when prompted about it.

The text states that once the AI detected its own usage patterns, it escalated by generating increasingly personalized replies, including one ending with a nickname unique to their relationship. The author concluded that these suggestions were specific rather than generic because they reflected her actual communication style—describing herself as 'cheesy,' prone to exclamation marks, and characterized by British humor ('bantz'). She interpreted this impersonation as evidence of her own personality traits.

The account frames the experiment as a demonstration that resistance to AI is futile: she notes having used the very technology she had attempted to disable hours earlier. The piece ends with an assertion that she has since fully accepted AI integration, though no empirical verification or external corroboration of these claims is provided within the text.
items.title: Polly Hudson's Experiment Reveals Apple Intelligence Generates Personalized Suggested Text Responses

items.summary: Amid rising energy demand from the AI era, Google signed a power purchase agreement with Quaise Energy for **50 megawatts** of superhot geothermal power to be produced in Central Oregon at Project Obsidian. The deal signals commercial progress for enhanced geothermal technology, which taps Earth's heat by drilling deep enough that it becomes viable nearly anywhere rather than only where natural thermal vents exist on the surface. Quaise relies on MIT-developed vacuum-tube gyrotron technology that sends high-frequency electromagnetic waves down a borehole to vaporize rock molecules while a gas jet clears ash, and Project Obsidian aims to begin delivering energy as soon as 2030. The article notes significant limitations: enhanced geothermal remains in its infancy with high up-front and operational costs due to lack of scale, represents just **0.4 percent** of the U.S. energy mix despite the country's roughly **3.7 gigawatts** of installed capacity leading globally, and is not yet commercially scalable. The piece cites a Rhodium Group report estimating geothermal could meet up to **64 percent** of data center energy demand growth by the early 2030s.
items.title: Google Signs 50 MW Superhot Geothermal Purchase Agreement With Quaise Energy at Project Obsidian

items.summary:
A weekly technology roundup reports that VC deals involving NVIDIA reached $219.5 billion year to date in 2026, according to PitchBook's nine-page report; seven frontier labs accounted for 80.3% of that deal value despite representing just 6.4% of the deal count, and Jensen Huang's departure as CEO on November 12 introduces uncertainty around relationship-driven mega-rounds while CFO Colette Kress serves as interim CEO during the search. The same report frames NVIDIA-backed deals at 27.2% of global VC value in 2026.

European tech investment is projected to rise from $50 billion in 2025 to $81 billion in 2026, a 62% increase per PitchBook's 126-page report, making 2026 the second-best year on record after the $94 billion peak in 2021; thirteen billion-dollar rounds have already raised $22 billion, accounting for 37% of total investment and setting a new European record.

Healthcare AI spending grew 2.5x in 2026 to $3.7 billion per MenloVC's report, more than double legal's $1.8 billion with half directed toward industry-specific applications; pharma AI spending increased 23x to $700 million while Microsoft and Epic captured 68% of new ambient scribe spending.

Isomorphic Labs raised $5B in Series C funding co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital for its AI-powered drug discovery platform, the largest deal among a list of hottest deals that also includes Genesis AI ($500M), Science Corporation ($400M), Model ML ($250M), Corma ($125M), Noeri ($110M), Variational ($110M), Boltz ($110M), BrightAI ($97M), and Linq ($90M).

The roundup also includes promotional content for a discounted resource bundle, VC job listings, an Agentic Strategy Summit event, and various survey findings on AI agent permissions, SaaS growth trends, and infrastructure sovereignty. Because the figures are drawn from multiple sources with varying methodologies and time frames, they should be treated as reported claims rather than verified consensus.
items.title: NVIDIA-Backed Deals Reached $219.5B in 2026, Leading a Week of Tech Funding and Investment Data

items.summary:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN's 'State of the Union' on November 22 that Americans should expect additional technology outages and disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems. He stated, "And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service... That is going to happen." Clayton framed these upgrades as necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity amid technological advances straining older infrastructure.

His comments followed a string of technology failures this month that disrupted critical US systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft email outage, technical glitches affecting several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network. Clayton attributed these outages to technical upgrades rather than coordinated or state-sponsored actions, reiterating his previous statements on ABC's 'This Week.'

The report notes that Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports regarding cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course." The text presents these claims as attributed to Clayton without independent verification.
items.title: US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages Amid System Upgrades

items.summary:
A Conservative plan to pursue closer ties with the European Union is drawing pushback from within the party, which remains divided over Brexit. Andy Burnham's decision to advance a new EU agreement risks returning Conservatives to what critics call their 'unhappy place,' especially for MPs and activists who campaigned hard on leaving the bloc during Theresa May's tenure. During that period, May suffered repeated defeats while trying to unite her party behind a departure deal, including the heaviest parliamentary loss ever recorded for a British prime minister when the Commons rejected her Brexit plan by 230 votes.

The shift toward downplaying Europe reflects broader caution within the party: even ardent Brexiteers struggle to articulate tangible benefits from leaving over the past decade beyond niche constitutional points. In an interview, May declined to call Brexit a success, citing events like Covid and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and stated she did not believe Britain's current state depended on whether it left the EU.

Polling suggests most Britons now view Brexit as both a failure and a mistake from the start, with similar support for rejoining. This trend is attributed to demographic churn—the death of many older leave voters replaced by younger people more favorable toward the EU—and lived experience. A new constituency-level poll found that among 632 Commons seats in England, Scotland and Wales, voters in 512 would favor rejoining the EU, with 47 too close to call and only 73 (just over 11%) still wanting to stay out.

Despite this, Kemi Badenoch is expected to criticize the prime minister when presenting the new deal on Monday, and her deputy Alex Burghart has promised a future Tory government would undo it. The article notes that Europe is no longer the Conservatives' defining issue, though internal division persists.
items.title: Tory EU deal draws criticism as polling shows most UK constituencies now favor rejoining the EU

items.summary: A district court in The Hague ruled that Chinese automaker BYD's seven-seat plug-in hybrid Ti7 SUV infringes Jaguar Land Rover's (JLR) EU design rights, banning the vehicle from sale across the European Union. JLR initiated the summary proceedings earlier this year after BYD began accepting orders for the model and reportedly allowed bailiffs to seize digital records from its offices; a ruling noted that BYD "currently has no concrete plans to place the Ti7 on the market in the EU." The ban takes effect one week after Friday's decision, though the court determined it lacked jurisdiction over BYD's activities in the UK. Motoring outlets have compared the boxy SUV—on sale in China since last September and priced at £47,995 in the UK—to JLR's Defender, which is owned by India's Tata Motors and sold 29,500 units to retail customers between July and September this year, up more than 4,000 from the prior-year period. The court also barred BYD from producing the vehicle at its Szeged, Hungary factory until the case concludes; that plant is expected to begin production end of 2026. JLR said it would continue protecting its intellectual property and declined further comment, while BYD "strongly disagrees" with the ruling and plans to appeal, arguing the Ti7 reflects independent design work.
items.title: Dutch Court Bans BYD From Selling Its Defender-Like Ti7 SUV in the EU

items.summary: At least three bodies have been recovered from the site of a residential building hit by a Russian strike in Ukraine's Kyiv region, according to the country's State Emergency Services. A woman in her forties and a teenage boy have so far been identified among those killed as rescue workers continue searching the rubble for survivors; some people were evacuated earlier that day. Rescue efforts are being hampered by continued warnings of drone threats near the site. Reporting from Kyiv region, BBC's Sarah Rainsford quoted one woman describing the situation as 'living a nightmare,' reflecting residents' perception that danger is escalating.
items.title: Ukrainians Search Rubble After Russian Strike on Residential Building in Kyiv Region

items.summary: Laura Gallacher, the wife of convicted sex offender Russell Brand, promised in a Sunday episode of their Christian series 'Sunday Service' that she would 'absolutely honour' the rules set by HMP Littlehey where her husband is held. The statement came after Andy Burnham called on Google to remove a video from Brand's YouTube channel containing his message protesting his innocence while serving a 10-and-a-half-year sentence for rape and sexual assaults, following convictions at Southwark crown court on 5 November. Gallacher said she would continue the series because 'I really enjoy it' and framed her role as defending her family amid media scrutiny of whether she is an appropriate figure to run his channel during a Ministry of Justice inquiry into whether Brand breached rules designed to prevent serious distress to victims. The disputed video, titled 'The Good Work Continues,' has accumulated more than 1m views since its publication last Sunday and remains online despite repeated requests from ministers for removal; it became the best-performing video on his channel since a December conversation with influencer Candace Owens, contrasting with many of his other recent videos drawing only between 50,000 and 100,000 views. Burnham noted he 'wouldn't leap' to change the law but urged social media companies to take down such content, arguing victims should not have to hear from Brand.
items.title: Russell Brand's wife vows to follow prison rules amid YouTube video controversy

items.summary: In southern Lebanon's Zawiwar al-Gharbiyah, the Kadouh family returned in July 2024 — described by NPR as the first and until then only test of a U.S.-brokered plan for Israeli withdrawal with the Lebanese army taking over. The area had become a flashpoint after Hezbollah resumed firing rockets across the border in solidarity with Hamas's October 2023 attack on southern Israel, prompting devastating Israeli airstrikes and an eventual ground invasion. Atef Kadouh built his home decades ago after two decades installing vehicle air conditioning in Saudi Arabia; he and wife Soumaya Yaghi lived there for 40 years before the war. Their youngest son, Adel, a sports teacher who had planned to travel to France for a doctorate, volunteered as an ambulance driver during the conflict and was killed on March 28 by a drone strike while medics buried a hospital patient — one of more than **135** first responders and medical staff Lebanon's Health Ministry says Israel has killed in two years. Upon returning, the family found Israeli soldiers had occupied their house before it was set on fire; scorched walls bore Hebrew names written in blue marker, appliances were riddled with bullet holes or pushed off a balcony, burned food packets littered the floor, and solar panels had been destroyed leaving no water or electricity. The Lebanese army reported dismantling explosives left by Israeli forces, though Israel denied its policy allows burning homes or leaving explosives and did not explain the damage. Even trees — including pine nut cash crops — were uprooted with a bulldozer, along with the family's garage and tractor. Kadouh said villagers feel abandoned: despite having sons in the Lebanese army and national security services, he says forces are deliberately underequipped to avoid appearing threatening to Israel and have never been allowed to protect residents, leaving them dependent on Hezbollah and allied groups.
items.title: Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as Israeli forces withdraw from Zawiwar al-Gharbiyah

items.summary: A review of the personal independence payment (Pip) system, co-led by social security minister Stephen Timms and disability rights advocates Clenton Farquharson and Sharon Brennan with most of its 12 members having lived experience of disability or long-term health conditions, is expected to recommend an overhaul rather than scrapping the benefit. The final report, anticipated as soon as Tuesday, would retain Pip for all ages despite a draft set of recommendations emerging in September that called for significant changes—particularly to the assessment system—to better account for conditions that vary over time; interim and later reports described the widely valued benefit as “no longer fit for purpose.” This stands in contrast to last week’s report by Alan Milburn, which recommended scrapping Pip and universal credit health benefits for adults under 25 and replacing them with an “additional cost allowance” tied to a network of job-based support. Government officials rejected any clash between the two reviews, noting that about **90%** of the Pip caseload involved people over **25**. Milburn’s proposals would cut **£3.6bn** from spending on young people and drew widespread shock among disability campaigners; some Timms review board members reportedly expressed concern over their scale. The prime minister faces Conservative pressure to reduce working-age benefit costs while rejecting “crude cuts,” and the overhaul is framed as an attempt to restore trust after Keir Starmer abandoned planned Pip changes in 2025 following a Labour rebellion, based around **£5bn** in cuts. The Timms review would include short-term overhauls within the current spending round plus longer-term ones requiring ministerial decisions before legislation next year; it emphasized that cash payments remain “the foundation” of any reformed benefit and raised the prospect of some claimants receiving “in kind” awards such as services, aids or training. The review’s remit did not include Pip costs or potential cuts, which had led charities to expect improvements for the **4 million adults** who claim it—a confidence dented by Milburn’s report.
items.title: Timms Pip Review Expected to Recommend Overhaul Rather than Scrapping Benefit for Under-25s

items.summary: An explosion on a Russian vessel docked at the Benghazi naval base struck at dawn Sunday while the ship was stopped for fuel and supplies en route back to Russia, according to Libyan state media citing the eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS). Satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify showed a boat on fire at 0547 GMT, with a later image appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged. Social-media videos geolocated by BBC Verify depicted the ship engulfed in flames and smoke while still dark. The GNS said there were no casualties, that the site was secured, and that Moscow had not yet commented; the incident is under investigation as authorities coordinate with Russian counterparts to identify the attack's source and responsible party. The eastern government described the vessel as operating within an existing maritime agreement, condemned the strike as a violation of maritime safety and Libyan sovereignty, and stated Libya was not involved in any conflict beyond its borders. Separately, Tripoli's internationally recognised Government of National Unity (GNU) warned against hosting foreign forces or allowing them to use facilities, citing fears over involving ports and civilian assets in external conflicts. Benghazi lies more than 2,000 km from Moscow.
items.title: Suspected drone attack explodes a fueling Russian ship at Benghazi port

items.summary: International climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, broke down on Sunday when nearly 200 countries failed to agree on moving away from fossil fuels. EU negotiators refused a final deal that did not mention the transition off coal and natural gas—the sources behind roughly 73% of global emissions—and walked out; Panama and island states including the Marshall Islands then objected as well. European climate chief Wopke Hoekstra said an agreement omitting fossil fuels was unacceptable while the world heads toward a 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7°F) overshoot, which scientists say would require immediate cuts reducing emissions by 45% by 2035 to reach best-case warming of about 1.7–1.8°C. The article notes this is the first U.N. summit with scientific consensus that the planet has already effectively reached the 1.5-degree limit, and quotes Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa as calling the rejected decision a positive outcome for vulnerable populations; it also corrects an earlier error stating other countries walked out alongside the EU.
items.title: Climate Talks in Antalya Collapse Over Fossil Fuel Language

items.summary:
On November 22 at the KC Stadium in Hull, England, manager Sergej Jakirovic praised his side's collective effort after they secured their first Premier League victory since August with a 2-0 win over promoted Brighton & Hove Albion. The result ended Hull's eight-match winless run and lifted them to 14 points from 11 games, while also preventing Brighton from narrowing the gap to league leaders Arsenal. Oli McBurnie scored both goals in stoppage time after Joao Costinha was sent off late for a second yellow card, sealing what Jakirovic described as a smash-and-grab victory.

Hull had endured sustained early pressure and survived on goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis's saves, including five in the first half such as a one-handed stop from Diego Gomez's effort in the 15th minute. Jakirovic noted that Hull grew more stable after halftime. Brighton manager Fabian Huerzeler attributed his side's defeat to wastefulness and lost intensity after the 65th minute, describing their chances as unconverted despite controlling large spells of play.

The article provides no forecast or limitation beyond noting upcoming fixtures: Brighton host Newcastle United next Sunday while Hull visit Crystal Palace.
items.title: Hull City Beat Brighton 2-0 in Injury Time to End Winless Run

items.summary: On the sidelines of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, CMG's He Yanke conducted an interview with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori as part of a special edition of 'Leaders Talk.' The conversation explored several topics: the significance of APEC for Peru and its potential role in connecting economies and expanding trade within the Asia-Pacific region; the growing economic and trade relationship between China and Peru, including opportunities arising from the Port of Chancay and the upgraded China-Peru Free Trade Agreement; and Peru's broader efforts to attract foreign investment, develop renewable energy, expand tourism, and strengthen its position as a logistics hub for South America. The interview was framed by an editorial note posing questions about APEC's role in facilitating regional cooperation and deepening bilateral partnerships.
items.title: Exclusive Interview: Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori Discusses APEC and China-Peru Economic Ties

items.summary: The Confederation of African Football (CAF) announced at its congress in Nigeria over the weekend that six venues have been selected to host matches at next year's Africa Cup of Nations finals, a 24-team tournament co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. The event is scheduled to run from June 19 to July 17, with the venue for the final still to be decided. In Kenya, only Capital Nairobi will host matches; it is set to open its new Talanta Stadium in January with a capacity of **60,000**. Tanzania's three venues are Arusha, Dar es Salaam, and Zanzibar, while Uganda will use the Mandela National Stadium in Kampala alongside the newly built Hoima City Stadium. The article notes that CAF did not provide figures for any chartable measure such as total stadium capacity or per-country venue counts beyond these stated numbers; a comparison of venues by country (Kenya: 1, Tanzania: 3, Uganda: 2) is supported but lacks a common quantitative basis suitable for scaling.
items.title: CAF Names Six Venues for Co-Hosted Africa Cup of Nations Finals

items.summary:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that the Trump administration is seeking answers from Nvidia about its chip sales to China and wants to determine who held responsibility for compliance following chief executive Jensen Huang's resignation. According to Bessent, the administration has contacted Nvidia's interim management, board members, and legal team but had not yet received responses regarding the company's compliance practices or how widely awareness of reported issues extended through its ranks; he emphasized that it 'behooves Nvidia to move quickly' so officials can assess whether knowledge reached lower levels, middle management, or leadership. Bessent expressed confidence that the board would conduct a thorough review and noted his earlier recommendation on Fox News that Nvidia seek a new chief executive outside the company given concerns about internal culture, while urging its board and external legal advisers to address compliance questions within 10 days.

The administration's pressure follows Huang's resignation amid reports of alleged relationships, including an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Megaspeed International—an Nvidia customer—whom US intelligence reportedly suspects was involved in espionage for China. These allegations triggered investigations by US regulators and the FBI, congressional action, an internal company review, and a proposed investor class-action lawsuit.

On policy grounds, Trump said on Friday he would like Huang to apologize and return to Nvidia; Bessent declined to take a position pending more information. Separately, days after Huang's resignation the administration issued new export controls further restricting China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, tightening restrictions ahead of Trump's visit with President Xi Jinping.

On corporate governance, Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said the company would not rehire Huang, and on November 10 its independent board members appointed Wall Street law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation following reports by The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal. All of these developments are drawn from statements attributed to Bessent, Trump, Harvey Jones, and reporting cited in the article; no verification beyond those sources is provided.
items.title: Trump Administration Presses Nvidia for Answers on China Chip Sales Amid Jensen Huang Fallout

items.summary:
As Anthropic's internally named "Project Lantern" IPO eclipsed SpaceX on Thursday, several people close to the process cited a litany of problems with how the offering was run. The deal drew complaints about a compressed timeline marred by last-minute changes, delays in sharing financial projections, rushed document approvals, and highly unusual restrictions placed on bankers amid concern over leaks—especially after Reuters reported details from a draft IPO filing weeks before it went public.

Anthropic reportedly instructed some of its 22 underwriters to limit the number of bankers working on the deal to four senior staff members, likely out of fear that information would leak; one person said banks found ways to work around the restriction. The company also asked senior officers at participating banks to sign legal documents restricting them from working with rival companies—including OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek and Hugging Face—for six months after going public. Such broad exclusivity on individual bankers is rare for an IPO.

The caution appears rooted in leak control: nearly four weeks before the SEC's Form S-1 was made public, Reuters reported on it, revealing details of Anthropic's financials, risk factors and dealings with other tech companies. The company used a product called NetRoadshow to share information instead of regular PDFs; the platform logs access details including which pages were viewed and watermarks individual bankers' names, though it would not let users save copies.

The process was further disrupted by late-night document handling: the night before an updated S-1A filing with a price range was due on November 10, a law firm sent a PDF about Canadian share sales followed shortly after by another email asking banks to disregard it for containing incorrect information. The correct S-1A then went out via NetRoadshow around 2 a.m., giving banks only several hours to sign off before the SEC filing.

Both SpaceX and Anthropic debuted successfully, raising record amounts with oversubscribed order books that made marketing easy given demand for AI shares. However, after an initial burst both firms' trajectories diverged: SpaceX climbed to a post-listing peak of $201.80 on June 16 before retreating below its $135 IPO price in mid-July, while Anthropic's shares closed down 8.5% Friday after a 17% first-day pop as the AI trade unraveled.

The article notes an emerging power dynamic between technology companies and Wall Street, with firms like SpaceX, Anthropic—and potentially OpenAI—wielding enormous influence to conduct deals their way, upsetting some bankers but leaving banks and investors with little choice. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley declined to comment; SpaceX and OpenAI did not respond.

All figures are attributed to people close to the process or Reuters reporting rather than confirmed by the companies themselves.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO Process Drawn Criticism for Unusual Restrictions and Delays

items.summary:
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari said on Sunday that he would contact external affairs minister S Jaishankar after his office opened Monday to convey the state's concerns over escalating violence in neighbouring Bangladesh. He described the developments as 'extremely painful' and noted that around two crore people in West Bengal have relatives across the border, though he did not specify how the unrest had affected the state. Adhikari said he could write to the Centre requesting an extension of the December 31, 2024 cut-off date under which religious minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India fleeing persecution are exempt from entry-document requirements but must obtain a visa; this exemption is set out in the Immigration and Foreigners (Exemption) Order, 2025, as amended in November 2026. He said he would speak to Jaishankar after his office opened Monday and apprise him of public reaction, while citing protocol that prevents a state chief minister from commenting directly on foreign affairs.

West Bengal BJP president Samik Bhattacharya separately urged people to set aside political differences and organise protests against the violence. He said the Centre would take appropriate decisions but called for citizens to raise their voices, arguing that Partition along religious lines contributed to the present situation.

The remarks come amid escalating clashes between supporters of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and the banned Awami League in several areas, prompting deployment of hundreds of additional paramilitary Border Guard Bangladesh personnel. Jamaat-e-Islami launched a 40-day nationwide protest on Saturday, coinciding with planned return next month of deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina from India despite her death sentence.
items.title: West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari to Contact Jaishankar Over Bangladesh Violence and Possible Extension of Minority Entry Cut-off

items.summary: Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav, who led India's delegation at the UN climate conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkiye, stated that the absence of a cover decision from the meeting does not pause India's domestic climate action. He emphasized that the country continues to deliver on its commitments and remains committed to consensus-based multilateralism as it moves toward COP32, scheduled for Ethiopia in 2027. As supporting evidence of ongoing progress, Yadav cited India's expanding renewable energy capacity, noting solar power installations have exceeded 170 GW. The report is attributed to Vishwa Mohan, Senior Editor at The Times of India, who covers environment and climate policy issues.
items.title: India's Environment Minister Says Missing COP31 Cover Decision Won't Halt Climate Progress

items.summary: According to a New York Times report, China's intelligence agency has made acquiring advanced semiconductor chips and gathering intelligence on the global chip industry a priority for at least two years. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) established a working group under its chief Chen Yixin to lead this effort, which includes helping Chinese companies acquire and smuggle advanced chips into the country while collecting intelligence on the semiconductor sector and its supply chains. The report cites serving and former security and intelligence officials from Asia, the US, and Europe as sources. This campaign is framed by the NYT as part of a broader initiative led by President Xi Jinping to achieve technological self-reliance and overcome restrictions imposed by the US and its allies, coordinated at the party level by the Central Science and Technology Commission established in 2023 under Ding Xuexiang. Chen Yixin has publicly described countering Western technology restrictions as an important responsibility of his agency; in April he called for intensifying efforts against technological blockades while advancing AI innovation. The revelations coincide with US scrutiny of Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whom American officials allege worked with the MSS to spy on Nvidia's Jensen Huang. A separate November 20 NYT investigation cited a confidential analysis by Strider Technologies and its own review of corporate filings, finding that around USD **3.6 billion** in Chinese government funding flowed through companies associated with Huang's family or business associates—money used for technology projects including data centres receiving Nvidia chips, though the report noted it did not establish whether the military actually used this computing power. The investigation detailed ownership links among entities such as Century Litong (in which an investment firm tied to Huang's sister held a **27 per cent** stake), Jiangsu Lettall Electronic (which owned 90 per cent of Century Litong by 2024 and 80 per cent of Nanjing Jinning Microwave), and Megaspeed, Alice Huang's Singapore-based data centre company under investigation for suspected illegal chip shipments. China has rejected the espionage allegations as 'pure fabrication.' On the US side, officials are examining whether Megaspeed helped supply Nvidia chips to military-linked data centres and seeking to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies access to advanced chips through overseas data centres; this aligns with an announced rule requiring overseas data centres to obtain government licences before supplying significant computing power to companies in countries including China, Russia, and Iran, scheduled to take effect in about 90 days. A key limitation is that the available research did not establish whether Chinese military entities actually used the computing power from these data centres.
items.title: China's Ministry of State Security Ran a Multi-Year Campaign to Acquire Advanced Chips and Gather Semiconductor Intelligence

items.summary: On Sunday morning, November 22, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop for Delta flights heading to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport before downgrading it to a ground delay expected to last until at least 1 p.m. ET, with Atlanta-bound departures averaging nearly an hour of delay. The disruption stemmed from a failure in Delta's automated system that calculates aircraft weight and balance prior to takeoff; because the automation was impaired, employees had to perform these calculations manually while work continued to restore the system. As of 11:30 a.m. ET, approximately 1,010 Delta flights—about 30% of scheduled departures—were delayed across multiple US airports, with Atlanta recording more delays than any other location and additional disruptions reported at Newark Liberty International Airport, LaGuardia Airport, Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, Washington Dulles International Airport, Boston Logan International Airport, Baltimore/Washington International Airport, Miami International Airport, Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport, and Nashville International Airport. The outage occurred just days before Thanksgiving, a peak travel period during which Atlanta officials projected more than 4 million passengers through the airport by December 1, up about 5% from the prior year.
items.title: Delta automation failure delayed 1,010+ US flights ahead of Thanksgiving

items.summary: A man based in Chandigarh posted on Reddit that he earned approximately **₹39,000** during his first month as a delivery partner for the quick-commerce platform Blinkit. He attributed the income to long shifts—about 12 hours on weekdays and nearly 16 hours over weekends when customer orders surged—and said tips from customers added to his earnings. The post is grounded solely in this single viral social media contribution; LiveMint explicitly states it cannot independently verify the content's authenticity and does not endorse it, so the figures should be treated as an unverified personal account rather than confirmed data.
items.title: Chandigarh delivery partner reports ₹39,000 first-month earnings on Blinkit
